month_card.sub: Summer's last heat and fall's first weight.

field_notes.name: The parking lot smells like September.
field_notes.body: For a few weeks, chiles get roasted in drum roasters outside markets across the Southwest, San Diego included. If you find one, buy a bag — it is cheaper than doing it yourself and better than you'd expect. If you don't, you already know how: the same dry pan from July, the same covered bowl from August. Chiles are just bigger and need longer. Char, steam fifteen minutes, slip the skins off, tear into strips.

field_notes.name: Salsa verde without a recipe.
field_notes.body: Husk and rinse a pound of tomatillos. Boil them until they turn from bright green to olive, about five minutes, or char them in a dry pan if you want smoke. Blend with a chile, a handful of cilantro, salt, and a squeeze of lime. That's it. There is no correct ratio — taste it and add whichever one is missing. It will be too sharp the first minute and right after ten.

field_notes.name: Don't peel the delicata.
field_notes.body: The skin is thin enough to eat, which is the entire reason to buy this squash instead of a butternut. Halve it lengthwise, scoop the seeds, cut into half-moons, toss with oil and salt, roast hot until the edges go dark. No peeler, no cleaver, no wrestling.

field_notes.name: September at the fish counter.
field_notes.body: In a warm year, dorado shows up off San Diego in late summer and stays into the fall. Yellowtail is still around. The question hasn't changed since July: not 'Do you have salmon?' but 'What came in today?' In September the counter often knows something you didn't plan for.

weekend_meal.name: Chiles rellenos, the plain way.
weekend_meal.intro: One meal should feel like the reason you went shopping. In September, it's the one you can only make while the chiles are here.
ingredients: 8 oz Monterey jack or Oaxaca cheese, cut into batons
1 can whole tomatoes, or 4 ripe tomatoes
weekend_meal.ingredient_note: The traditional version is battered in whipped egg and fried. It's worth doing once, and it is not what this is. Roasted, stuffed, and baked gets you most of the way there on a Sunday afternoon.
weekend_meal.method: Char the poblanos on all sides — burner, grill, or dry pan. Steam them covered for fifteen minutes, then slip off the skins, keeping the chiles whole. Cut one slit down each side and pull out the seeds. Blend tomatoes, onion, and garlic; simmer in a little oil with salt until it darkens slightly, about twenty minutes. Tuck cheese into each chile, set them in a baking dish, and bake at 425°F until the cheese gives, about fifteen minutes. Spoon the broth around them, not over them. Cilantro and lime at the table.

drink.name: Golden Hill Agua Fresca
drink.intro: One drink. Make it while the grapes are cheap.
drink.method: Blend the grapes with a cup of cold water for about fifteen seconds — no longer, or the seeds and skins turn it bitter. Pour through a fine-mesh strainer, pressing gently. Add another cup of cold water, the juice of half a lime, and a pinch of salt. Taste: it should be barely sweet. Pour over ice with a lime wedge.

local_ritual.label: San Diego ritual
local_ritual.name: Drive up to Julian.
local_ritual.description: An hour inland and four thousand feet up, the apples come in while the coast is still in shorts. Go on a weekday if you can. Buy more than you meant to, eat one in the car, and notice that it is genuinely cooler up there — the first cool air of the year most San Diegans get.

one_thing_to_notice.headline: The stripes on a delicata.
one_thing_to_notice.body: A delicata's green stripes deepen toward orange as it cures. Pale ones were picked recently and taste closer to summer squash. The ones with real orange down in the grooves have had time, and they're sweeter. Both are worth eating. They're just not the same squash.

guides.name: Jerome
guides.voice: Direct, welcoming, practical. Has a strong opinion about which lap to buy on.
guides.notices: What is at its peak this week versus what is being pushed. What the farmers themselves are eating.

quotes.delicata-squash: First squash of the year always outsells the good squash in November. Buy it anyway. It's a different pleasure.
quotes.apples: An apple that traveled three days is a fine apple. An apple that came down the mountain yesterday is a different fruit.
quotes.grapes: Cheapest they'll be. Buy twice what you'd normally buy and keep them cold.
quotes.edition: September is two markets in one aisle. Half of it is leaving and half of it is showing up.

guides.voice: Unhurried, funny about how much heat people claim they can take.
guides.notices: Skin that blisters evenly. The moment a tomatillo turns from bright green to olive. Whether the cilantro was cut this morning.

roasting-chiles.name: Roasting chiles
roasting-chiles.tile_uses: Rice bowls, tacos, pasta, the weekend meal
roasting-chiles.why_now: Poblanos, Anaheims, and Hatch chiles come in together in late August and are gone by mid-October. This is the short window when they are everywhere, cheap, and often being roasted in a drum outside the market. Nothing else in the year replaces them.
how_to_choose: Firm, glossy, and heavy for their size
Flat-ish sides char more evenly than deeply lobed ones
Poblano for stuffing — wide shoulders, thick walls
Anaheim or Hatch for strips — longer, thinner, milder
Skip anything wrinkled or light; it has been sitting
roasting-chiles.buy_this_much: 6–8 for the week. They lose about half their volume once roasted and peeled, so this is less than it looks.
roasting-chiles.price_note: Cheapest they will be all year, and cheaper still by the sack. If a market is roasting them on site, that price usually beats buying them raw and doing it yourself.

flavor_paths.name: Rajas
flavor_paths.description: Roasted, peeled, torn into strips. The default. Into everything all week.

flavor_paths.name: Creamed
flavor_paths.description: Blended with cream or Greek yogurt into a sauce for pasta or chicken.

flavor_paths.name: Stuffed
flavor_paths.description: Whole poblanos, cheese, a simple tomato broth. The weekend meal.

weekday_uses: Strips folded into a rice bowl
Strips in tacos with escabeche and lime
Blended with cream for pasta
Chopped into scrambled eggs
roasting-chiles.weekend_use: Chiles rellenos: charred, peeled, stuffed with jack cheese, baked, and set in a simple tomato broth.
roasting-chiles.storage: Whole and raw, a week in the crisper. Roasted and peeled, four days in the fridge in a covered container, or freeze them in strips — they freeze better than almost any other vegetable in this basket.
roasting-chiles.one_thing_to_learn: Charring a chile is not about cooking it. It is about destroying the skin, which is thin, papery, and unpleasant to eat, so that what is underneath can be. That is also why the covered fifteen minutes after charring matters more than the char itself: the trapped steam separates skin from flesh. Skip the steam and you will spend ten minutes scraping. Do it, and the skin slips off in sheets.
roasting-chiles.market_question: Are these Hatch, or grown here? And how hot is this batch?

tomatillos.name: Tomatillos
tomatillos.tile_uses: Salsa verde, tacos, rice bowls, chicken
tomatillos.why_now: Tomatillos run from midsummer into October and are at their best right now — heavy, tight in the husk, and tart in a way that no other ingredient in the basket is. They are also the cheapest sauce you can make from scratch.
how_to_choose: The husk should be tight and papery, not shriveled or loose
The fruit should fill its husk completely
Firm, with a slight tackiness underneath — that is normal, rinse it off
Bright green, not yellowing; yellow means sweeter and duller
Small ones are usually tarter than large ones
tomatillos.buy_this_much: 1 lb. That is one batch of salsa verde, which is about a week's worth.
tomatillos.price_note: Inexpensive year-round and especially now. A pound of tomatillos makes more salsa than a jar of it costs.

flavor_paths.name: Boiled
flavor_paths.description: Simmered until olive-colored, then blended. Softer, rounder, the everyday version.

flavor_paths.name: Charred
flavor_paths.description: Blistered in a dry pan first. Smokier and darker. The July technique, again.

flavor_paths.name: Raw
flavor_paths.description: Blended straight, uncooked. Sharpest of the three. Good on rich meat, hard on eggs.

weekday_uses: Salsa verde on rice bowls
Salsa verde on tacos
Simmered with chicken thighs until the sauce thickens
Spooned over fried eggs
tomatillos.weekend_use: Simmer a pot of chicken thighs in salsa verde for an hour and shred them. It is the easiest thing in this edition and it feeds you for days.
tomatillos.storage: Leave the husks on and keep them in a paper bag in the crisper — two weeks, easily. Husked, they go sticky and soft faster. Blended salsa keeps five days.
tomatillos.one_thing_to_learn: Tomatillos are not unripe tomatoes. They are a different plant, related to the ground cherry, and the sourness is structural rather than a sign that you got there too early. That means you cannot fix a tomatillo by waiting. What you can do is decide how much of that sharpness you want: raw keeps all of it, boiling rounds it off, charring trades some of it for smoke.
tomatillos.market_question: Were these picked this week? And do you cook yours or use them raw?

cilantro.name: Cilantro
cilantro.tile_uses: Salsa verde, tacos, rice bowls, beans
cilantro.why_now: Cilantro is a cool-weather herb. It bolts and turns bitter in July heat, and it comes back as the nights start to drop. September is the handoff: basil is on its way out, cilantro is on its way in, and this month's basket is built around the second one.
how_to_choose: Deep green leaves with no yellowing at the edges
Stems firm, not limp or slimy at the cut
No flower buds — a bunch that has bolted will taste soapy and thin
Smell it. If it smells like nothing, it has been in a cooler too long
A bunch with roots attached, if you can find one, keeps twice as long
cilantro.buy_this_much: 1 large bunch. You will use more of it than you expect, because the stems count.
cilantro.price_note: One of the cheapest ingredients you can buy at any store. If a bunch looks tired, buy two — it costs almost nothing to be generous with it.

flavor_paths.name: Blended
flavor_paths.description: Stems and all, into salsa verde. This is where most of the bunch goes.

flavor_paths.name: Torn on top
flavor_paths.description: Leaves only, after the heat. Tacos, bowls, beans, eggs.

flavor_paths.name: Stirred into yogurt
flavor_paths.description: Chopped fine with lime and salt. A cold sauce for anything charred.

weekday_uses: Blended into salsa verde, stems included
Torn over rice bowls at the table
Stirred through a pot of beans off the heat
Chopped into yogurt with lime for a cold sauce
cilantro.weekend_use: Scattered over the chiles rellenos with a lime wedge — the only green thing on the plate, and it should be a lot of it.
cilantro.storage: Trim the stem ends, stand the bunch in an inch of water like flowers, and put a bag loosely over the top in the fridge. Ten days instead of three. Change the water when you think of it.
cilantro.one_thing_to_learn: The stems are not scraps. They carry more of the flavor than the leaves and none of the fragility, which is why they belong in anything blended or simmered while the leaves belong on top at the last second. Learning to split the bunch — stems into the blender, leaves into a bowl for later — is the whole technique, and it applies to parsley the same way.
cilantro.market_question: Was this cut this morning? Do you have any with the roots still on?

limes.name: Limes
limes.tile_uses: Salsa verde, tacos, the drink, everything
limes.why_now: California limes are harvested from late summer through winter, and early fall is when they are heaviest with juice and cheapest at the register. Every other ingredient in this basket is sharpened by one. In September a lime is not a garnish — it is a seasoning you buy by the bag.
how_to_choose: Heavy for its size — that is juice
Thin, smooth skin rather than thick and pebbled
A little yellow at the blossom end is fine and often means riper and juicier
Give it a gentle squeeze; it should have some give
Skip hard, light, dark-green ones — they are dry inside
limes.buy_this_much: 5–6 for the week. One goes into the salsa, one into the drink, and the rest get squeezed over whatever you made.
limes.price_note: Cheapest in late summer and fall. Bagged limes are usually a better deal than loose ones and are fine for juicing, if not for wedges.

flavor_paths.name: Squeezed at the table
flavor_paths.description: The last thing that happens to almost every plate this month.

flavor_paths.name: In the blender
flavor_paths.description: Into salsa verde, to keep it green and stop it tasting flat.

flavor_paths.name: Zested
flavor_paths.description: Over fruit, yogurt, or the drink. All the aroma, none of the acid.

weekday_uses: Squeezed over tacos and rice bowls
Into salsa verde at the end, to taste
Whisked with olive oil and salt as a two-ingredient dressing
Over cut fruit with a pinch of salt and chile
limes.weekend_use: Wedges on the table with the chiles rellenos. The broth is rich and the lime is what keeps you eating.
limes.storage: Loose in the crisper drawer, not on the counter — two to three weeks cold versus one week warm. Juice keeps five days in a jar, or freeze it in an ice cube tray.
limes.one_thing_to_learn: Acid is a seasoning, and it does a job salt cannot. When a bowl of beans or a pot of salsa tastes finished but somehow flat, the missing thing is almost never more salt — it is a squeeze of lime. Learn to reach for that first, and half the food you cook gets better without a single new ingredient.
limes.market_question: Are these Persian or key limes? Which ones are juicier right now?

delicata-squash.name: Delicata squash
delicata-squash.tile_uses: Rice bowls, tacos, roasting alongside chicken
delicata-squash.why_now: The first winter squash of the year shows up at the end of September, and delicata is the one worth buying while it is still hot outside. It is smaller, sweeter, and faster than the squash that comes in November, and unlike them, you do not have to peel it.
how_to_choose: Cream-colored with green stripes — orange in the grooves means longer cured and sweeter
Firm all over, with no soft or wet spots at either end
Heavy for its size
A dry, intact stem still attached
Small to medium; the large ones get watery
delicata-squash.buy_this_much: 2 squash. That is two dinners' worth of roasted half-moons, or one dinner and a week of rice bowl additions.
delicata-squash.price_note: Usually sold by the piece rather than by weight, which makes the medium ones the better buy. Early-season squash costs a little more than it will in November.

flavor_paths.name: Roasted plain
flavor_paths.description: Half-moons, oil, salt, hot oven. The version you will actually make.

flavor_paths.name: Roasted with chile
flavor_paths.description: Tossed with chile strips at the end. Sweet against smoke.

flavor_paths.name: Charred and dressed
flavor_paths.description: Roasted hard, then hit with lime and cilantro while still hot.

weekday_uses: Roasted half-moons over rice
Folded into a taco with chile strips and escabeche
Roasted on the same sheet pan as chicken thighs
Cold from the fridge, on yogurt with salt and lime
delicata-squash.weekend_use: A whole tray roasted dark alongside chicken, with the escabeche jar on the table. Almost no work, and it makes the kitchen smell like the season changed.
delicata-squash.storage: On the counter, out of the sun, for a month — it does not need the fridge and does better without it. Once cut, wrap and refrigerate, and use within four days.
delicata-squash.one_thing_to_learn: Winter squash is sweeter than it looks, and the way to find that out is heat and space. Cut it thin, oil it well, spread it out with room between the pieces, and roast it at 425°F or higher until the edges go genuinely dark — not golden, dark. Crowd the pan and it steams into something soft and bland. It is the same lesson eggplant taught in August, on a different vegetable.
delicata-squash.market_question: How long has this been cured? Do you have any with more orange in the stripes?

apples.name: Julian apples
apples.tile_uses: Raw, slaw on tacos, yogurt, cheese
apples.why_now: Julian is an hour inland and four thousand feet up, and its apples come down the mountain starting in September. A local apple picked this week and eaten raw is a completely different fruit from one that has been in cold storage since last fall — crisper, sharper, and more fragrant.
how_to_choose: Firm all over, with no give when you press near the stem
Smell the blossom end — a fresh apple smells like an apple
Skin should be taut, not waxy or slippery
Small bruises are fine; soft brown patches are not
Ask what came in this week rather than choosing by variety
apples.buy_this_much: 4–5 for the week, and buy more than that if you actually drive up. They keep.
apples.price_note: Mountain apples cost more than the bin at the grocery store, and for the first few weeks of the season they are worth it. By November, the difference narrows.

flavor_paths.name: Raw and cold
flavor_paths.description: Sliced, salted if you like. This is where most of them should go.

flavor_paths.name: Shredded
flavor_paths.description: Into a slaw with lime and cilantro. On tacos, it is a revelation.

flavor_paths.name: With something salty
flavor_paths.description: Sharp cheddar, or a sandwich. Sweetness against salt.

weekday_uses: Grated over yogurt with honey
Shredded into a quick lime-and-cilantro slaw for tacos
Sliced with cheddar and sourdough for lunch
Eaten whole, cold, in the afternoon
apples.weekend_use: A slaw of shredded apple, cabbage, lime, salt, and a lot of cilantro, on the table next to anything you charred.
apples.storage: Refrigerate them. A cold apple keeps for a month and stays crisp; a counter apple goes mealy in a week. Keep them away from anything that absorbs smells.
apples.one_thing_to_learn: Apples are one of the few things in the produce aisle where nothing is truly out of season — but almost everything is out of harvest. Most of the year you are eating fruit that has been held in controlled cold storage for months, which is impressive and also why supermarket apples taste the same in March as in December. September and October are the weeks when you can taste the difference, and the only way to notice it is to eat one raw.
apples.market_question: What came down from the mountain this week?

grapes.name: Table grapes
grapes.tile_uses: The drink, yogurt, cheese, eaten cold
grapes.why_now: California table grapes peak from late August through October, and September is when the good ones get cheap. This is the one thing in the basket that asks nothing of you — no technique, no recipe, no heat. Buy them, keep them cold, eat them.
how_to_choose: Green stems, not brown and brittle — that is the freshness tell, not the fruit
Grapes firmly attached; if they fall off the bunch, it is old
A dusty white bloom on the skin is a good sign, not dirt
Plump, with no shriveling where they meet the stem
Taste one if the market allows it. Sweetness does not increase after picking
grapes.buy_this_much: 1–2 lbs. One pound gets eaten; the second one becomes the drink.
grapes.price_note: The cheapest weeks of the year for grapes. Prices climb again by late fall when the domestic season ends and imports take over.

flavor_paths.name: Cold and plain
flavor_paths.description: Straight from the fridge. Do not overthink this one.

flavor_paths.name: Blended
flavor_paths.description: Into agua fresca with lime and a pinch of salt.

flavor_paths.name: With salt and cheese
flavor_paths.description: Alongside something sharp on a board. Sweet against salty and cold.

weekday_uses: Cold, by the handful
Halved over yogurt with honey
Blended into the agua fresca
Frozen on a tray and eaten like candy
grapes.weekend_use: On a board with sharp cheese, sourdough, and the apples — twenty minutes of assembly for people who came over.
grapes.storage: Unwashed, in their bag, in the coldest part of the fridge. Rinse only what you are about to eat; washed grapes turn soft in a day.
grapes.one_thing_to_learn: Grapes do not ripen after they are picked. Unlike the peaches and figs of the last two editions, a hard, sour grape stays a hard, sour grape on your counter forever, which is why the stem tells you more than the fruit does. Green, flexible stems mean the bunch came off the vine recently. Brown, dry, brittle stems mean weeks in a cooler, no matter how good the grapes still look.
